summary: Dissociative anesthetic that, in psychiatry, is used off-label for rapid relief in severe treatment-resistant depression and, in acute settings, for severe agitation when standard meds fail. Fast onset, powerful effects, and real monitoring requirements.
description: Ketamine is best known as an anesthetic, but in psychiatry it’s sometimes used off-label for treatment-resistant depression because it can work within hours instead of weeks. It can also be used in emergency settings for severe, dangerous agitation when benzodiazepines and antipsychotics haven’t worked. Ketamine can cause dissociation, vivid perceptual changes, blood pressure spikes, and rare breathing problems—so it’s not a “take-at-home” med in most cases. This is a monitored-medication lane, not a casual one.

primary.condition_name: Depressive episode (severe, treatment resistant) associated with major depressive disorder (unipolar) (off-label)

off_label.context: Used off-label for severe, treatment-resistant depressive episodes when multiple standard treatments (meds and/or therapy) have failed. Often delivered as a monitored IV infusion series; effects can be rapid but durability varies and ongoing plan still matters.

Used off-label in acute care settings for severe or refractory agitation when benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics have failed, especially when safety is an immediate concern and rapid sedation is required.

therapeutic_response.display: IV anesthetic effect within ~30 seconds; IM within ~3-4 minutes; psychiatric infusion protocols commonly use slow IV administration over ~40 minutes

common_adverse_effects.effect: Emergence reactions (dreamlike state, hallucinations, delirium-like confusion)
common_adverse_effects.incidence: ≥10% reported in labeling for prolonged emergence phenomena (varies widely by setting/dose)
common_adverse_effects.notes: This can look like vivid dreams, perceptual distortion, agitation, or confusion during recovery. A calm environment helps. Fast IV pushes and higher doses increase risk. Some clinicians use a benzodiazepine to treat severe reactions, but premedication can prolong recovery.
Feeling detached from your body, time distortion, or intensified sensory input can happen during dosing. In depression protocols, slower infusions are often used to reduce the whiplash effect.

common_adverse_effects.effect: Increased blood pressure and heart rate
common_adverse_effects.notes: Ketamine often increases sympathetic tone—BP and pulse can jump quickly and usually settle within minutes after peak. This matters a lot if you have uncontrolled hypertension or heart disease.
Can occur during or after dosing. Clinics often plan around this (hydration, anti-nausea meds if needed).
Even when it’s not used as a full anesthetic, it can still impair coordination and judgment. No driving, no risky decisions, no “let me just run errands after.”

serious_risks.risk: Respiratory depression or apnea (rare; higher risk with rapid IV administration, IM dosing, overdose, or co-use of other CNS depressants): MEDICAL EMERGENCY if unresponsive or breathing is slowed.
Severe emergence delirium (agitation, hallucinations, confusion) that threatens safety: may require medical management and a low-stimulation recovery setting.
Cardiac decompensation or arrhythmia in vulnerable patients (especially if myocardial dysfunction or significant coronary disease): requires monitoring and risk assessment.
Urinary tract injury with chronic/repeated exposure (ketamine cystitis, bladder dysfunction, hematuria, hydronephrosis): can become persistent if not addressed early.
Liver/biliary injury with recurrent or continuous use (cholestatic pattern, biliary duct changes, sclerosing cholangitis reports): evaluate symptoms and labs if long-term or repeated treatments.

contraindications.contraindication: Hypersensitivity to ketamine or any component
Conditions in which an increase in blood pressure would be hazardous
Known or suspected schizophrenia (commonly listed as an absolute contraindication for ED procedural sedation use due to risk of psychiatric destabilization)

precautions: Requires clinical monitoring: heart rate, blood pressure, breathing, oxygen saturation, and level of sedation
Respiratory depression/apnea can occur (rare but real), most associated with rapid IV administration, overdose, IM dosing, or combining with other CNS depressants
Cardiovascular effects: often raises blood pressure and heart rate; can be risky when increased BP would be hazardous
Emergence reactions: vivid dreams, hallucinations, delirium-like confusion can occur during recovery and up to 24 hours
Genitourinary toxicity with chronic/repeated use: urinary urgency, frequency, pain, hematuria; cystitis and bladder dysfunction have been reported with long-term exposure (especially misuse)
Liver injury with recurrent or continuous use has been reported (cholestatic patterns, biliary changes, sclerosing cholangitis reports)
Misuse/dependence risk exists, especially with repeated exposure, dose escalation, and substance use history
Psychiatric destabilization risk: can worsen psychosis-like symptoms in vulnerable patients; avoid or use extreme caution in patients with known/suspected schizophrenia

interactions.interactant: Other CNS depressants (benzodiazepines, opioids, alcohol, sedating antihistamines, sleep meds)
interactions.mechanism: Additive sedation, impaired airway reflexes, and increased risk of respiratory depression/apnea. Can also worsen confusion or delirium during recovery.
interactions.action: Avoid alcohol. Use extreme caution with sedatives. If co-administration is medically necessary, dosing and monitoring must be clinician-directed in a supervised setting.

interactions.interactant: Stimulants and sympathomimetics (including some ADHD meds and decongestants)
interactions.mechanism: May amplify increases in blood pressure and heart rate.
interactions.action: Clinician should review meds and vitals. Consider holding nonessential sympathomimetics around treatment time depending on protocol and patient risk.

interactions.mechanism: May change ketamine and active metabolite exposure (effect and side effects can shift unpredictably).
interactions.action: Medication review matters. If you’re on strong enzyme modifiers, dosing and monitoring plans may need adjustment.

monitoring_requirements.parameter: Vital signs during and after dosing: heart rate, blood pressure, respiratory rate, and oxygen saturation
Level of sedation and airway status, especially with higher doses or when combined with other sedatives
Emergence reactions: agitation, confusion, hallucinations; maintain a low-stimulation recovery environment and have a plan for severe reactions
Cardiac monitoring in patients at risk from blood pressure/heart rate increases (eg, known coronary disease, heart failure, uncontrolled hypertension)
Mood and safety monitoring for depression treatment: symptom scales, suicidality checks, functional improvement, and relapse prevention planning
Urinary symptoms with repeated exposure: dysuria, urgency, frequency, hematuria; evaluate early to prevent persistent bladder injury
Liver labs with repeated or prolonged use: LFTs, alkaline phosphatase, and gamma-glutamyl transferase at baseline and periodically if treatment is ongoing
Misuse risk screening: escalating use, cravings, nonmedical use patterns, diversion risk, and co-occurring substance use disorders
Medication review for interaction risks: sedatives (respiratory depression), sympathomimetics (BP/HR), and CYP modifiers (exposure changes)

special_populations.pregnancy: Ketamine crosses the placenta. Large doses around delivery have been associated with dose-related neonatal depression and lower Apgar scores, and ketamine can increase uterine contractions (effects may vary by trimester). The manufacturer does not recommend obstetric use, though ketamine has been studied in obstetric anesthesia and as adjunct analgesia in some settings. For psychiatric depression treatment, weigh severity of illness, alternatives, and the risks of untreated depression using shared decision-making. Repeated or prolonged exposure to anesthetic/sedation agents in pregnancy (especially when procedures are lengthy, eg >3 hours) has been associated with potential neurodevelopmental risk signals based on animal data and FDA warnings; human data are limited and not definitive.
special_populations.lactation: Ketamine and metabolites are present in breast milk. Available case reports/series suggest low relative infant doses after maternal ketamine infusions or injections, and some reports did not observe adverse events in infants, but data are still limited. In general, breastfeeding may resume once the mother is awake, stable, and alert after anesthesia; extra caution is warranted for infants at higher risk of apnea/hypotonia. For repeated ketamine treatments for depression while breastfeeding, decision-making should consider infant age, dosing schedule, maternal benefit, and monitoring for sedation or feeding issues.
special_populations.geriatric: Older adults can be more vulnerable to falls, confusion, and hemodynamic stress. Some prescribing-safety frameworks consider ketamine potentially inappropriate for depression in adults ≥65 due to fall risk. If used, start with cautious protocols, monitor vitals closely, and prioritize safety (mobility support, low stimulation recovery, careful medication interaction review).
special_populations.renal_impairment: Parenteral: no initial dose adjustment is generally required, but steady-state concentrations may be higher in severe kidney dysfunction and metabolites (eg, dehydronorketamine) can accumulate; avoid prolonged use or monitor for toxicity with repeated/prolonged exposure. Oral (off-label): no initial adjustment suggested, but oral PK data are limited and first-pass metabolism yields higher metabolite exposure; use caution and close monitoring in severe kidney impairment.
special_populations.hepatic_impairment: No specific manufacturer labeling adjustments provided. Because ketamine is hepatically metabolized, use caution in liver disease and consider closer monitoring if repeated or prolonged courses are used; recurrent/continuous exposure has been associated with hepatobiliary lab abnormalities and cholestatic patterns.

pharmacokinetics.absorption: Route-dependent; IV has immediate bioavailability; IM is high; oral is low due to first-pass metabolism
pharmacokinetics.bioavailability: IM ~93%; oral ~20-30%; intranasal ~35-50% (variable by device and technique)
pharmacokinetics.peak_plasma: IM ~5-30 minutes; intranasal ~10-20 minutes; oral ~30 minutes
pharmacokinetics.metabolism: Extensive hepatic metabolism primarily via CYP2B6 and CYP3A4 to norketamine (active) and other metabolites (eg, hydroxynorketamine, dehydronorketamine)

dosing.titration: Psychiatric ketamine dosing is off-label and protocol-driven. The best-studied depression approach is a monitored IV infusion. For severe agitation in emergency/ICU settings, ketamine is used as a rapid sedative when standard meds fail. Doses below are examples from clinical guidance; local protocols vary and monitoring is required.

discontinuation.taper_guidance: Ketamine isn’t typically “tapered” the way SSRIs or benzodiazepines are when it’s used as an intermittent infusion series. That said, with prolonged or frequent use, tolerance and dependence can occur, and withdrawal symptoms have been reported after stopping—especially in misuse scenarios or long-term high-dose exposure.

sections.heading: What It's Used For
sections.text: Ketamine is an anesthetic medication, but in psychiatry it’s used off-label in two very specific lanes: (1) rapid treatment for severe, treatment-resistant depression, and (2) emergency sedation for severe agitation when usual options don’t work fast enough or haven’t worked at all. This is not a casual, everyday antidepressant—this is a monitored medication with real physiologic and psychological effects.
items: {link:condition:major-depressive-disorder:Treatment-resistant major depressive episodes (unipolar)}: Off-label rapid antidepressant strategy, most commonly delivered as a monitored IV infusion series
{link:condition:agitation:Acute, severe, or refractory agitation}: Off-label use in emergency/ICU settings when benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics have failed
off_label: Treatment-resistant depression protocols using IV ketamine infusion (most studied route)
Severe agitation requiring rapid sedation in acute care settings
Adjunct sedation/analgesia in ICU settings (psychiatry-adjacent when agitation is part of the problem)

sections.heading: What People Feel

items.category: Rapid mood shift (hours to 1 day, depression protocols)
quotes: It didn’t feel like happiness—it felt like the heaviness lifted enough that I could function.
My suicidal thoughts got quieter fast. Not magically gone, but no longer screaming.
It was like my brain finally stopped looping the same dark track.

items.category: Dissociation / “out-of-body” feeling (during and shortly after dosing)
quotes: I felt disconnected from my body, like I was watching myself from far away.
Time got weird. A few minutes felt like an hour.
I knew I was safe, but I felt like I was floating in a different room of reality.
items.note: Dissociation is common and dose-related. This is a big reason ketamine is usually given with monitoring and a calm recovery environment.

quotes: Colors looked louder. Sounds felt too close.
I had vivid images, like a half-dream with my eyes open.
It wasn’t scary, but it was intense—like my senses got turned up.
items.note: Emergence reactions can include vivid dreams, hallucinations, and delirium-like confusion—especially with higher doses or fast IV pushes.

quotes: Afterward I felt drained, like my brain ran a marathon.
I was a little foggy for the rest of the day.
I felt emotionally open—sometimes in a good way, sometimes raw.
It knocked the chaos down fast.
I went from unsafe to calm in minutes.
I don’t remember much, but I stopped fighting and could be cared for.
items.note: In severe agitation, the goal is rapid control of dangerous behavior and physiologic stabilization—this is a different use-case than depression protocols.

sections.intro: Ketamine is one of those meds where the experience is part of the medication. Some people feel relief; others feel thrown into a weird dream-like state. Here’s what people commonly describe:

sections.heading: How Fast It Works
sections.text: Ketamine is fast. How fast depends on what you’re using it for and how it’s given. In psychiatry, the key difference is whether you’re using a slower antidepressant-style infusion or rapid sedation dosing for severe agitation.
key_points: Depression protocols: commonly given IV over ~40 minutes (less abrupt experience vs IV push)
Anesthetic/sedation duration: IV effect ~5-10 minutes; IM effect ~12-25 minutes (recovery can be longer)
Psychiatric antidepressant effects: can show up within hours to 1 day in responders; durability varies (often days to a week without a continuation plan)
Rare respiratory depression/apnea risk is most associated with rapid IV administration or combination with other CNS depressants

sections.heading: How Well It Works
sections.text: Ketamine is not a classic daily antidepressant. It’s a rapid-acting intervention sometimes used when depression is severe and stubborn. Many protocols use a monitored IV infusion and repeat dosing (often weekly or multiple times per week early on). Some people feel a noticeable shift quickly; others don’t respond, or the benefit fades without a structured continuation strategy.
sections.clinical_details: In psychiatric practice, IV ketamine for treatment-resistant depression is typically delivered as a slow infusion (commonly 0.5 mg/kg over 40 minutes) with repeat sessions based on response and tolerability. Treatment courses up to ~6 weeks have been studied, but optimal duration and maintenance strategy are not fully defined. Ketamine may be used alongside oral antidepressants and psychotherapy rather than replacing them.

patient_counseling: This is not a “drive yourself home” med. If you’re receiving ketamine for depression, plan to be monitored and to have someone get you home.
Avoid alcohol and sedatives on treatment days unless your clinician explicitly approves—stacking sedation increases risk.
Tell your clinician if you have heart disease, uncontrolled hypertension, aneurysm history, or anything where a BP spike is dangerous.
Tell your clinician if you have a history of psychosis, mania, or schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms.
If ketamine is being used repeatedly, report urinary symptoms early (burning, urgency, frequency, blood in urine). Don’t “push through” that.
For depression treatment: ketamine isn’t a stand-alone plan. The goal is fast symptom relief plus a real long-term strategy (therapy, meds, lifestyle, relapse plan).

sections.heading: Side Effects
sections.summary: Ketamine’s side effects are a mix of body stuff (blood pressure, nausea) and brain stuff (dissociation, vivid dreams). Most are dose-related and more likely when given quickly or in higher doses.
plain_language_list: Dissociation (feeling detached from body or surroundings)
Vivid dreams, hallucinations, confusion during recovery (emergence reactions)
Increased blood pressure and heart rate
Dizziness, unsteadiness, slowed reaction time (don’t drive after)
Rare: breathing slowing or brief apnea (more risk with rapid IV dosing or other sedatives)

sections.intro: Ketamine can stack dangerously with other sedatives and can be affected by medications that change CYP metabolism (especially CYP2B6 and CYP3A4). In psychiatry, the biggest practical issue is additive sedation and cardiorespiratory risk when combined with other CNS depressants.

sections.heading: Safe Discontinuation
sections.text: Ketamine isn’t typically “tapered” the way SSRIs or benzodiazepines are when it’s used as an intermittent infusion series. That said, with prolonged or frequent use, tolerance and dependence can occur, and withdrawal symptoms have been reported after stopping—especially in misuse scenarios or long-term high-dose exposure.
key_points: In depression protocols, ketamine is often given as time-limited treatments (eg, a series over weeks) and then spaced out or stopped based on response.
With prolonged or high-frequency exposure, dependence and tolerance have been described; withdrawal symptoms can start within ~24 hours after stopping and may last ~3 days (sometimes up to 2 weeks).

Reported withdrawal symptoms can include shaking, sweating, palpitations, fatigue, decreased appetite, chills, autonomic arousal, restlessness, cravings, dysphoria, anxiety, depressed mood, nightmares, paranoia, delusions, and hallucinations.
If someone has been using ketamine frequently (medical or nonmedical), discontinuation should be clinician-supervised with monitoring for withdrawal, relapse of depression, and safety risks.

sections.heading: Dosing Information
sections.text: Psychiatric ketamine dosing is off-label and protocol-driven. The best-studied depression approach is a monitored IV infusion. For severe agitation in emergency/ICU settings, ketamine is used as a rapid sedative when standard meds fail. Doses below are examples from clinical guidance; local protocols vary and monitoring is required.

adult.depression_trd_iv_infusion: 0.5 mg/kg IV infused over 40 minutes; may repeat 1 to 3 times weekly; may increase to 0.75 to 1 mg/kg based on response and tolerability; treatment courses up to ~6 weeks have been studied
adult.depression_trd_im: 0.25 to 0.5 mg/kg IM per dose (data limited; frequency varies by protocol and is less standardized than IV)
adult.agitation_severe_adjunct_iv: 1 to 2 mg/kg IV once over 30 to 60 seconds; if sedation is inadequate, may repeat once after 5 to 10 minutes with 0.5 to 1 mg/kg (repeat dosing is uncommon if the initial dose is at the high end)
adult.agitation_severe_adjunct_im: 4 to 6 mg/kg IM once; if sedation is inadequate, may repeat once after 10 to 25 minutes with 2 to 3 mg/kg; maximum recommended IM dose: 400 mg
adult.administration_safety: To decrease risk of respiratory depression and apnea, administer IV bolus doses over >30 to 60 seconds (avoid rapid pushes). In depression protocols, infusion is typically over 40 minutes.

sections.simple_explanation: For depression, ketamine is usually given as a slow, monitored IV infusion to reduce abrupt dissociation and to keep vitals stable. For severe agitation, dosing is higher and designed to work fast—this is typically an emergency/ICU use case with close monitoring.

sections.heading: Pregnancy, Breastfeeding, Special Groups

In pregnancy, it’s generally not a first-choice medication for psychiatric treatment, but medically necessary procedures should not be withheld solely due to pregnancy. For depression treatment, reproductive status should be discussed up front as part of shared decision-making.

sections.heading: Available Formulations
sections.text: Ketamine (Ketalar) is most commonly used as an injectable solution. In psychiatry, IV infusion is the most studied route for depression protocols. Other routes (intranasal, oral, subcutaneous) show up in some settings but are less standardized and often off-label.
items: Injection solution (Ketalar): 10 mg/mL, 50 mg/mL, 100 mg/mL (vial sizes vary)
Generic ketamine injection solutions: 10 mg/mL, 50 mg/mL, 100 mg/mL
Off-label use: Intranasal administration using injectable solution and an atomizer/device (dose limited by nasal volume)
Off-label use: Oral administration using injectable solution mixed with a flavoring agent (variable absorption, higher metabolite exposure)

sections.heading: Mechanism of Action
sections.text: Ketamine is a noncompetitive NMDA receptor antagonist that blocks glutamate signaling. At higher doses it produces a dissociative, cataleptic-like state—your brain feels separated from the environment. At lower, subanesthetic doses, it can modulate central sensitization and hyperalgesia, and in psychiatry it’s thought to rapidly shift synaptic signaling and plasticity in circuits involved in depression. The exact antidepressant mechanism isn’t fully settled, but the clinical effect can be fast.

sections.heading: Place in Treatment Algorithm
sections.text: For depression, ketamine is typically considered when the episode is severe and treatment-resistant—after standard first-line and second-line approaches (medications, therapy, combined strategies) haven’t produced adequate relief. It’s often used as a rapid intervention to reduce symptom severity quickly while a longer-term plan is built or optimized. For agitation, ketamine is an acute-care tool: it’s for situations where someone is severely agitated, unsafe, and not responding to benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics—where speed and safety drive the decision.

faqs.a: Ketamine is not FDA-approved as an antidepressant. It’s a general anesthetic that’s used off-label in psychiatry for severe, treatment-resistant depression because it can work fast in some people—sometimes within hours to a day. Off-label doesn’t mean “wrong,” but it does mean it’s protocol-driven and usually monitored.

faqs.q: How fast does ketamine work for depression?
faqs.a: In responders, ketamine can reduce depressive symptoms and suicidal thinking within hours to 24 hours after an infusion. Not everyone responds, and the effect can fade without a continuation plan. It’s often used as a rapid intervention while longer-term treatments are optimized.

Many people feel dissociation—like they’re detached from their body or surroundings—plus time distortion and dreamlike imagery. Some people find it calm or neutral; others find it intense or unsettling. Clinics usually use a low-stimulation setting and monitoring to keep the experience safer and smoother.

faqs.q: What’s the typical ketamine dosing for treatment-resistant depression?
faqs.a: A commonly studied protocol is 0.5 mg/kg IV infused over 40 minutes, repeated 1 to 3 times per week early in treatment. Some protocols increase to 0.75 to 1 mg/kg based on response and tolerability. Courses up to about 6 weeks have been studied, but optimal duration and maintenance strategy are still evolving.

faqs.q: Can ketamine be used for severe agitation?
faqs.a: Yes, in acute care settings ketamine may be used off-label for severe or refractory agitation—especially when benzodiazepines and/or antipsychotics have failed and rapid sedation is needed for safety. Dosing is higher than depression protocols and requires airway-capable monitoring.

faqs.q: Is ketamine safe to mix with alcohol or benzodiazepines?
faqs.a: Mixing ketamine with alcohol, opioids, or other sedatives increases the risk of dangerous oversedation and breathing problems. If ketamine is being given in a monitored clinical setting, clinicians may sometimes use other sedatives intentionally, but that’s a supervised decision—not a DIY combo.

faqs.q: Why do clinics monitor blood pressure during ketamine?
faqs.a: Ketamine often raises blood pressure and heart rate through sympathetic stimulation. For many people it’s temporary, but if you have uncontrolled hypertension, coronary artery disease, aneurysm risk, or heart failure, that spike can be dangerous—so monitoring isn’t optional.

faqs.q: Can ketamine cause addiction or withdrawal?
faqs.a: Ketamine can cause tolerance and dependence with repeated or prolonged use, and withdrawal symptoms have been reported after discontinuation—especially in heavy or long-term use patterns. That’s one reason responsible psychiatric use is structured, monitored, and not open-ended.

faqs.q: What are the biggest red-flag side effects?
faqs.a: Breathing problems (rare but urgent), severe confusion/agitation during recovery, chest pain or dangerous blood pressure elevations, and urinary symptoms (burning, urgency, blood in urine) during repeated use. If urinary symptoms appear, don’t ignore them—early evaluation matters.

faqs.q: Can you drive after ketamine treatment?
faqs.a: No. Ketamine can impair coordination, judgment, and reaction time, and emergence effects can linger. Most protocols require you to have a responsible adult take you home and avoid driving or hazardous activity for at least the rest of the day (often 24 hours in anesthesia contexts).

faqs.q: Is ketamine okay in pregnancy or breastfeeding?
faqs.a: Ketamine crosses the placenta and is present in breast milk. In pregnancy it’s generally not a first-choice psychiatric medication, but medically necessary procedures shouldn’t be withheld solely due to pregnancy. For breastfeeding, limited data suggest low infant exposure in some cases, but decisions should weigh infant age/risk and the treatment plan, and should be guided by your clinician.
